newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Berisha meets European experts as U.N. mulls force.
newsitem.headline: Berisha meets European experts as U.N. mulls force.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha met European relief experts on Friday and the government hoped separately for a quick U.N. decision to approve a multinational force to guard aid supplies after a slide towards chaos.

Berisha met a delegation headed by senior Dutch diplomat Jan de Marchant et d'Ansembourg for talks in central Tirana on the crisis in the former communist state tormented by gangsterism and insurrection.

United Nations Security Council members met informally late on Thursday night in New York to consider an Italian request to send a force to help protect humanitarian aid shipments to Europe's poorest country.

But, while most delegations were in favour of endorsing a force in principle, they hesitated on giving quick approval without details of its mandate, its duration and who would pay, several council members said.

Greece, France, Spain, Portugal, Austria, Turkey and Romania have expressed willingness to take part. Italy has estimated that about 2,500 personnel would be deployed initially, with another 2,500 in reserve.

Meanwhile, Albanian police were investigating the killings of 18 people in a shootout in central Albania on Thursday night, the worst bloodletting in two months of crisis, an interior ministry source said.

He said that a pile of 17 corpses were discovered in Levan, apparently a group of gunmen killed by local residents to avenge the shooting of a local leader. He said that 14 of the dead had been identified as coming from the southern towns of Vlore, Fier, Tepelene and Memaliaj.
Much of southern Albania is ruled by rebels or armed gangs who blame right-wing Berisha for the collapse of popular savings schemes in recent months in which thousands of people lost everything.
The killings added to a death toll of already well over 100 people. Most military depots have been looted and prisoners released. Most foreign nationals were evacuated this month.
The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) on Thursday asked the U.N. to consider endorsing a force comprising volunteer nations.

Diplomats said that passing the issue to the United Nations might delay approval for any force and that the move reflected unease at the OSCE, especially by Russia, about endorsing use of armed missions to a member state.
Albanian officials have repeatedly urged the quickest possible action by foreign nations to agree to a force to help protect ports.
D'Ansembourg has said any force could range up to about 3,000 personnel -- police, gendarmes or military police.
He said he was "was especially going to discuss the election issue with Mr Berisha". Berisha signed a pact with a new unity government on March 9 calling for elections by June.
D'Ansembourg said Justice Minister Spartak Ngjela had suggested a slight delay, telling him that "June might be too early while August would be too late."
Also on Friday, the International Committee of the Red Cross was renewing efforts to transport aid overland into southern Albania in a test of perilous roads held by bandits.
Two Red Cross vehicles returned into Greece after waiting in vain for several hours at a southern border post on Thursday for word from relief workers that it was safe to cross.
"They were due to leave early this morning for another try. The problems they had at the border yesterday have been cleared up," Red Cross spokeswoman Amanda Williamson said.

In a sign of the weak grip of the central authorities, the self-styled "salvation committee" in the southern town of Vlore was planning to hold talks on the crisis on Friday with political groups, diplomats and representatives of international groups based in Albania.
A bank in Vlore was burnt down on Thursday night by robbers who broke into the main safe. After leaving they set fire to the building, where smaller safes were broken into a day earlier.
